strengths: Novel geometric characterization of feasible classifiers under sufficiency, with elegant connection to fractional knapsack and piecewise hyperbolic boundary structure
Addresses practically important gap in prior work by handling finite-valued score distributions rather than requiring continuity and full support
Rigorous mathematical framework with complete proofs; properly handles intersection of subgroup-feasible regions and provides clear algorithmic procedures
General optimization framework accommodates arbitrary loss functions and multiple objectives (loss minimization, deviation from separation), not limited to specific problems
Well-written presentation with clear mathematical exposition and effective visualizations; honest treatment of limitations including degenerate cases
Exact solution rather than approximation; methodologically sound with thorough treatment of edge cases
weaknesses: Severely limited empirical validation: single COMPAS dataset with no baseline comparisons, marginal accuracy improvement (0.677 vs 0.681), and no ablation studies or sensitivity analysis

Strong input assumption requiring group-calibrated scores, but paper provides no guidance on obtaining such scores in practice or handling approximate calibration; COMPAS example uses 20% of data just for calibration

Practical impact unclear—COMPAS results show different group-specific thresholds which practitioners likely already apply; no demonstration that exact optimal solution substantially outperforms simpler heuristics

Scope limited to binary classification and sufficiency constraint; generalization to multiclass or other fairness notions not discussed; known incompatibility with separation is acknowledged but not deeply explored
Computational complexity of Algorithm 1 not explicitly stated; COMPAS example shows the two optimization objectives often coincide without explanation of when/why they diverge
Missing technical details on numerical stability, finite-sample verification of group-calibration, and detailed baseline comparisons that would establish practical relevance

strengths: Solid theoretical contribution: Provides rigorous geometric characterization (Theorems 3.3-3.4) of the feasible region for finite-valued group-calibrated scores, extending prior work (Baumann et al. 2022) that required continuity assumptions.
Practical problem formulation: Addresses finite-valued, group-calibrated scores as arise in real systems like COMPAS, removing unrealistic continuity requirements.

Complete algorithmic framework: Algorithm 1 efficiently traces the boundary of the feasible region and optimizes multiple objectives (loss minimization, separation-deviation minimization) with clear pseudocode.
Technically mature treatment: Includes handling of degenerate cases, comprehensive appendices with detailed proofs, and analysis of multiple fairness objectives.
Clear exposition: Well-written with helpful visualizations (Figures 1-3) and good use of geometric intuition to explain the feasible region structure.
weaknesses: Critically insufficient experimental validation: Only one use case (COMPAS) with minimal detail; no comparisons with Baumann et al. (2022), Canetti et al. (2019), or simple baselines; no synthetic experiments; no computational complexity analysis. This is a major gap for ICML.

Unrealistic core assumption inadequately addressed: The method assumes perfectly group-calibrated scores, which is extremely difficult to achieve in practice. No robustness analysis of calibration errors, no sensitivity study, and no practical guidance on achieving group-calibration. The COMPAS example uses empirical calibration on 20% of data with unquantified noise impact.

Incremental novelty: The main contribution is extending from continuous to finite-valued scores—necessary but somewhat incremental. Missing direct experimental comparison with Baumann et al. (2022) on finite data. The geometric approach via feasible regions is standard in constrained optimization.

Narrow scope with limited practical guidance: Binary classification and binary protected attribute (extensions claimed but not demonstrated); post-processing only; no discussion of when practitioners should adopt sufficiency over competing fairness notions; unclear practical deployment scenarios.

Superficial treatment of sufficiency-separation incompatibility: Problem is identified but Section 6's solution (minimize separation deviation under sufficiency) lacks empirical validation, tradeoff analysis, or practical guidance. The COMPAS example shows optimizers coincide, providing no insight.

Missing critical comparisons: No comparison with the most related work (Baumann et al. 2022) on finite-valued data; no comparison with Corbett-Davies et al.'s group-specific thresholding or Canetti et al.'s abstention methods. Unclear what practical advantages the proposed method offers.

Reproducibility and implementation gaps: No code provided; COMPAS calibration procedure sparse (random stratified split without seed details); missing sample complexity analysis for group-calibrated score estimation; no ablation studies on robustness to bin count, group imbalance, or partial support overlap.

Limited experimental scope: No timing/scalability analysis; only 0-1 loss evaluated (no domain-specific loss discussion); no sensitivity analysis to calibration error magnitude; single dataset insufficient to validate generality.
